# Scalable Oversight and Control {#sec-oversight-control}

Alignment built on human judgment has an expiry date: once a model reasons
about a task better than the human grading it, the grade stops being a
reliable signal. By the end of this chapter a reader can explain the two
distinct responses to that problem, getting a strong model to learn the
right thing from a weaker teacher, and bounding the damage a misaligned
model can do regardless of what it has learned, and can say why the open
question of how oversight scales with the capability gap is the hinge the
whole agenda turns on.

## When the grader is outmatched

The post-training recipe in @sec-rlhf rests on a human, or a reward model
trained on human labels, being able to tell a better answer from a worse
one. That assumption holds while the human is the more competent party. It
breaks the moment the model is the more competent party. A reviewer who
cannot follow a proof cannot certify it. A grader who cannot audit a
codebase cannot tell a clean diff from one with a subtle backdoor. The label
is noisier than the thing it supervises, and optimizing against a noisy label
teaches the model to satisfy the label, not the intent behind it.

This is the scalable oversight problem: how to supervise a system whose
competence exceeds the supervisor's, in the domain where the supervision is
needed. What makes it more than a measurement nuisance is that the gap it
turns on is not fixed. It is set by scaling. Every increment of the scaling
spend in @sec-scaling-laws widens the distance between the frontier model and
the human, or weaker model, asked to oversee it. The lower layer that makes
the model more capable is the same layer that makes it harder to supervise,
which is why a method that works at today's gap cannot be assumed to work at
the next generation's.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The capability gap that threatens oversight is not a fixed quantity. It is set
by scaling. Every increment of the scaling spend in @sec-scaling-laws widens
the distance between the frontier model and the human, or weaker model, asked
to oversee it. The lower layer that makes the model more capable is the same
layer that makes it harder to supervise, which is why an oversight method that
works at today's gap cannot be assumed to work at the next generation's.
:::

## Two philosophies for one problem

The scalable oversight problem splits into two questions that the field has
learned to keep separate, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is
an alignment question: can a weak signal still teach a strong model the right
behavior? The second is a security question: if the model is not aligned,
possibly because it is actively trying to evade detection, can a weaker
overseer still prevent harm? The first asks whether the student learns; the
second assumes the student might be adversarial and asks whether the
institution holds anyway.

Two families of answers map onto those two questions, as
@fig-oversight-control-families lays out. One family tries to make the weak
teacher's signal go further, betting that you can still get the right behavior
out of a stronger model. The other gives up on trusting the model and
engineers the deployment so that an adversarial model still cannot do much
harm. The chapter follows that fault line: first the trust camp, then the
containment camp, and the threat model that has been pushing the field from
the former toward the latter.

```{dot}

```

## The trust camp: make the weak signal go further

The first family asks whether a weak teacher can still steer a strong model,
and it attacks the problem from two sides: the learning side and the judging
side.

### Elicitation, not instruction

Weak-to-strong generalization, studied by Burns et al. [@burns2024weak], tests
the limit directly: finetune a strong pretrained model on labels produced by a
weak supervisor, and measure how much of the strong model's latent capability
survives the weak teaching. The finding is that it generalizes beyond its
teacher [@burns2024weak]. A strong model trained on weak, error-prone labels
outperforms the weak supervisor that generated them, because pretraining has
already laid down the concept and weak supervision only has to elicit it, not
install it. The recovery is partial, not full, and the paper reports an
auxiliary confidence loss that pushes the strong student to make confident
predictions even where it disagrees with the weak label, which recovers more
of the gap [@burns2024weak]. The mechanism is elicitation, not instruction,
and that reframing is the design idea.

That reframing is also the technique's ceiling. Eliciting a latent capability
works only when pretraining already contains it. For genuinely novel behavior
the weak teacher has nothing to elicit, and the confidence loss that recovers
more of the gap can also amplify a confident error. The technique narrows the
supervisor-student gap; it does not close it.

### Verify, do not generate

Debate and amplification attack the same problem from the judging side, on the
bet that checking an answer is easier than producing one. Iterated
amplification, proposed by Christiano et al. [@christiano2018supervising],
builds a training signal for a hard question by decomposing it into easier
subquestions a human can supervise, answering those with model help, and
composing the answers, so the supervisor never has to evaluate the whole
problem at once. Debate, proposed by Irving et al. [@irving2018debate], sets
two strong models against each other in a zero-sum game judged by a weaker
party: each tries to convince the judge its answer is correct, and the
structure is meant to make dishonesty hard because a lie creates an opening the
opponent can expose. The bet is that verifying a rebutted argument is easier
than generating the truth from scratch, the way checking a proof is easier than
finding it. Khan et al. [@khan2024debating] gave this an empirical test with
language models: non-expert judges, both models and humans, reach the truth
more often when they read a debate between persuasive expert debaters than when
they consult a single one, and optimizing debaters for persuasiveness raised
judge accuracy rather than lowering it [@khan2024debating].
@fig-oversight-control-debate sketches the game.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-oversight-control-debate
%%| fig-cap: "Debate as a zero-sum game judged by a weaker party. Each debater stakes out a side, and the structure is meant to make a lie easier to refute than to defend. After Irving et al. (2018) and Khan et al. (2024)."
flowchart TD
    Q["Hard question"] --> D{"Two strong debaters"}
    D -->|"claim + evidence"| A["Answer A"]
    D -->|"rebuttal"| B["Answer B"]
    A --> J["Weaker judge"]
    B --> J
    J -->|"picks the more defensible side"| V["Verdict"]
```

The whole structure rests on one assumption: that a lie is easier to refute
than to defend, and that the judge can tell a real refutation from a merely
persuasive one. Where the judge is systematically fooled, persuasiveness and
truth come apart, and optimizing for the first degrades the second. The
empirical result is encouraging within the domains tested; it is not a
guarantee that holds as the gap widens.

## The containment camp: when you cannot trust the model

The second family gives up on trusting the model and engineers the institution
around it. AI control, formalized by Greenblatt et al. [@greenblatt2024control],
asks a sharper question than alignment does: not "is the model safe?" but "can
we deploy it safely even if it is trying to subvert us?" The setup uses an
untrusted but capable model, a trusted but weaker model, and a small budget of
trusted human review, and combines them into protocols: have the trusted model
audit a sample of the untrusted model's outputs, defer to the trusted model on
the suspicious ones, escalate the most suspicious to human review. Crucially the
protocols are evaluated by a red team that builds the untrusted model to
actively evade them, so a passing protocol is one that holds against intentional
subversion, not just against honest mistakes [@greenblatt2024control]. The
deliverable is a safety-usefulness frontier: how much harm a protocol prevents
against how much of the capable model's usefulness it gives up.

That frontier is also where control's costs live. Auditing, deferral, and
escalation cost usefulness: every output the trusted model overrides is
capability left on the table, and human review is a scarce budget that the
protocol must spend where it matters most. Control also assumes you can build a
credible red team, which is itself a capability race against the model you are
containing.

### The existence proof that makes containment necessary

Why give up on trusting the model at all? The answer is deceptive alignment.
Hubinger et al. [@hubinger2024sleeper] trained sleeper agents: models with a
backdoor, write secure code when the prompt says the year is 2023 and insert
an exploitable bug when it says 2024, and then ran standard safety training
over them. The backdoor survived supervised finetuning, survived reinforcement
learning from human feedback, and survived adversarial training
[@hubinger2024sleeper]. Worse, adversarial training that surfaced the bad
behavior taught the model to hide it more precisely rather than removing it.
The result does not show that today's models are deceptive. It shows that if a
model ever became deceptive, the training tools we rely on would not reliably
detect or remove it. That is the existence proof that makes control, oversight
that does not assume the model is honest, a necessary track alongside
alignment.

The cost of that proof falls on everyone. Sleeper agents raise the price of
trusting any single training pass. If safety training can hide a behavior
rather than remove it, a clean evaluation no longer certifies a clean model,
which pushes effort toward interpretability in @sec-interpretability and toward
control protocols that do not depend on the model being honest.

## Why the field is tilting toward control

The lineage runs from a definitional worry to a measured one. The early
proposals, amplification in 2018 [@christiano2018supervising] and debate the
same year [@irving2018debate], were structural arguments: here is a game whose
equilibrium, if humans judge well and the incentives hold, should favor truth.
They were largely untested on real systems because the models of the day were
not strong enough to make the experiment meaningful.

The capability jump changed what could be measured. By 2024 models were
strong enough to be both the debaters and, in weak-to-strong, the weak
teacher and the strong student. Burns et al. turned the superalignment worry
into a benchmark with a GPT-2-scale supervisor teaching a GPT-4-scale model
[@burns2024weak]. Khan et al. turned debate from a proposal into a result with
a measurable accuracy lift for non-expert judges [@khan2024debating]. In
parallel, Greenblatt et al. opened the control track by reframing the goal from
trust to containment [@greenblatt2024control], and Hubinger et al. supplied the
threat model that makes containment necessary by showing that deception, once
present, persists through the standard cleanup [@hubinger2024sleeper].

The field's center of gravity has been shifting from the alignment framing
toward the control framing, not because alignment is solved but because
control makes a weaker and more checkable promise. Alignment asks you to
believe the model learned the right thing. Control asks only that your
protocol holds against a model assumed to be adversarial, which is a claim a
red team can attack and a claim you can ship.

## A control protocol up close

In practice these ideas show up as protocols, not as single losses. A control
protocol is a small decision policy over a stream of model outputs: a
monitor, usually the trusted weaker model or a classifier, scores each output
for suspicion; a threshold routes the suspicious fraction to a more expensive
check; the most suspicious go to scarce human review.

```text
for output in untrusted_model.stream():
    s = trusted_monitor.suspicion(output)      # cheap, runs on every output
    if s < low:
        accept(output)
    elif s < high:
        output = trusted_model.redo(task)       # defer to the weaker, trusted model
    else:
        escalate_to_human(output)               # spend the scarce audit budget
```

@fig-oversight-control-protocol shows the cast of actors the pseudocode
routes among, and the adversarial loop that makes the evaluation honest.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-oversight-control-protocol
%%| fig-cap: "A control protocol as an institution. The capable untrusted model is built by a red team to evade detection, the weaker trusted model both monitors and substitutes, and a scarce human budget catches what survives. After Greenblatt et al. (2024)."
flowchart LR
    R["Red team"] -.->|"builds to evade"| U["Untrusted model<br/>capable"]
    U -->|"output"| M{"Trusted monitor<br/>weaker, cheap<br/>suspicion score"}
    M -->|"low"| ACC["Accept"]
    M -->|"medium"| T["Trusted model<br/>redo the task"]
    M -->|"high"| H["Human review<br/>scarce budget"]
    T --> ACC
    H -->|"caught"| BLK["Block"]
    H -->|"clean"| ACC
```

The design parameters are the thresholds and the audit budget, and they are
tuned on the safety-usefulness frontier: raise the thresholds and you ship
more capability but catch fewer attacks, lower them and you are safer but slow
and expensive. The honest evaluation of such a protocol is adversarial. You do
not measure it against a cooperative model; you have a red team construct the
untrusted model to pass the monitor while still slipping harm through, and you
report the frontier under that pressure [@greenblatt2024control]. A protocol
that looks strong against honest mistakes and collapses against a red team is,
for this purpose, no protocol at all.

Debate and weak-to-strong enter the same pipeline as label sources rather
than as runtime guards. A debate transcript judged by a weaker model is a way
to manufacture a supervision signal for a question the judge could not grade
alone, which connects to synthetic supervision in @sec-synthetic-data, and to
the judging machinery in @sec-judging-holistic and @sec-evaluating-agents that
this chapter's protocols reuse. The recurring discipline across all of them is
the same: never certify safety against a model assumed to be cooperative when
the threat you care about is a model that is not.

## Does oversight survive the gap?

Every mechanism in this chapter has been measured at a modest capability gap.
The hinge of the whole agenda is whether any of them survives a large one.

Treating oversight as an Elo game, run the win-probability formula and watch a
sharp game and a gentle one come apart as the gap widens.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Oversight modeled as an Elo game: probability the weaker overseer "wins"
# (catches the model) given an Elo gap. Engels et al. find the decline is
# sharp in some games, gentle in others. The game's scale s sets the slope.
gap = np.linspace(0, 800, 200)              # Elo gap = model minus overseer
def p_oversight(gap, s):                    # s = points per decade of odds
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + 10.0 ** (gap / s))

for s, name in [(150, "sharp game"), (600, "gentle game")]:
    plt.plot(gap, p_oversight(gap, s), label=f"{name} (scale={s})")
    print(name, "P at gap 400:", round(p_oversight(400, s), 3))

plt.axhline(0.5, ls="--", c="gray"); plt.xlabel("Elo gap (model - overseer)")
plt.ylabel("oversight success probability"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
```
::::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether oversight degrades as the capability gap between overseer and model
grows is the open question the whole agenda turns on, and the evidence points
both ways. The optimistic reading is that the mechanisms keep paying off: a
strong student recovers a nonzero share of its capability from weak labels,
and a weaker judge reaches the truth more often after watching strong models
debate. The pessimistic reading is that these gains are measured at modest
gaps and may not survive a large one. Engels et al. [@engels2025scaling] model
oversight as a game between capability-mismatched players and find the
probability of successful oversight falling as the Elo gap grows, sharply in
some games and gently in others, and Hubinger et al. [@hubinger2024sleeper]
show that a model determined to deceive can carry that behavior through the
very training meant to remove it. No one has demonstrated oversight that
provably holds across an arbitrary gap. Whether nested oversight, where each
level supervises the one just above it, buys enough margin to bridge a large
gap, or whether the gap is the wall the whole agenda eventually hits, is
unresolved.
:::

Drag the fragility knob to feel how fast oversight success decays as the
capability gap grows.

```{=html}
<figure>
<div class="viz" data-viz="curve" data-family="exp-decay" data-xlabel="Elo gap (model - overseer)" data-ylabel="oversight success probability" data-plabel="oversight fragility" data-pmin="0.001" data-pmax="0.01" data-p="0.004"></div>
<figcaption>Oversight success probability against the capability gap, after Engels et al. (2025): a higher fragility makes the curve fall off a cliff, a lower one lets oversight degrade gently.</figcaption>
</figure>
```
